title: An Egg for Tobi
summary: Tobi finds an egg all alone by the river and decides to look after it, even though nobody in the valley thinks he can.

scenes.text:
In a wide green valley lived a young dinosaur called Tobi.

He wasn't big yet. His neck only just reached the lowest branches, and when he ran, his legs got in a tangle.

Tobi lived with his herd: lots of long-necked dinosaurs who ate ferns, bathed in the river and slept all together in the clearing.

There were Cresta and Roco, the two noisiest youngsters in the valley, who always ran everywhere.

And there was Grandma Duna, the oldest of them all, who never ran anywhere.

Tobi liked his days. In the morning he drank at the river. At midday he ate ferns. At night he fell asleep snuggled up against the others, nice and warm.

Until one morning, he walked a little further than usual, following the stream.

Between two wet stones, in a hollow of soft earth, there was something that wasn't a stone.

It was round, the colour of sand, with blue spots.

It was an egg.

Tobi brought his snout close and sniffed it. It smelled of moss and river. And it was still warm.

He looked one way. He looked the other. There was nobody there. No mummy, no daddy, not a single footprint.

Tobi sat down to wait. He waited while the sun climbed. He waited while a blue dragonfly landed on his tail. He waited so long that his tummy rumbled three times.

But nobody came.

The sky turned grey. And Tobi thought: if night comes, it'll get cold. If the water rises, it'll be swept away.

Very carefully, he lifted it with his front legs and held it against his chest.

"I won't leave you on your own," he told it. "I'll look after you."

When Tobi got back to the clearing, the whole herd lifted their heads.

Cresta and Roco came running over.

"An egg!" said Roco, roaring with laughter. "Tobi, you don't know how to look after eggs. You can hardly look after yourself!"

"It'll get cold," said Cresta. "Or it'll break. Eggs are for mummies."

Tobi's cheeks went hot. But he hugged the egg a little tighter.

Then Grandma Duna came over, slowly, the way she did everything.

She looked at the egg. She looked at Tobi. And she said, in her voice like smooth stone:

"Looking after isn't something you know, little one. It's something you learn. And you learn it by looking after."

The next day, Tobi began to learn.

First he left the egg in the sun. But the sun moved across the sky, and the egg ended up in the shade, cold as a stone.

Then he covered it with dry leaves. But a breeze came and blew them all away.

Tobi felt like crying. That was when Grandma Duna taught him the secret.

"Leaves underneath. Warm earth around the sides. And your body on top, like a roof. Now breathe slowly, so the egg learns your rhythm."

Tobi lay down on top, very carefully, and took a breath.

Slowly. Very slowly.

And he felt the egg rise and fall with his chest, as if the two of them were breathing together.

The days went by, and Tobi learned lots of things.

He learned to turn the egg every so often, so it warmed up on all sides. He learned to fan it with his tail when it was very hot. He learned to sing it the only song he knew, croaky and out of tune, which sounded like water running over stones.

"You'll come out soon," he would say. "And I'll show you the whole valley."

One night, while everyone was asleep, Tobi felt something new.

A knock.

Soft, from the inside. As if someone were tapping on a very tiny door.

"Is that you?" whispered Tobi.

And the egg moved again, just a little. That night, Tobi hardly slept at all, he was so excited.

That week, the sky turned dark and heavy with clouds.

First came a few big, separate drops. Then the rain poured down all at once.

The whole valley lit up with a flash of lightning.

Tobi felt scared, a small, cold fear right at the tip of his tail. But he remembered that little sound from inside the egg, and the fear got smaller than him.

He lay down over the nest, stretched out his neck, tucked in his legs and made a roof out of his own body.

All night long the rain fell on his back. And all night long Tobi stayed still, soaked through, looking after.

Underneath, the egg stayed dry and warm.

When the sun came out, the valley wasn't the same any more.

The river had burst its banks and reached all the way to the clearing. Water ran between the ferns, and the big tree's roots were underwater.

Grandma Duna sniffed the air.

"It's going to keep rising," she said. "We're leaving today for the high plateaus, where the river can't reach."

The herd lined up. Cresta and Roco went first, splashing.

Tobi stayed behind for a moment. His nest was now a tiny island in the middle of the water.

He lifted the egg very carefully and tucked it into the hollow of his chest, between his front legs.

"We're going on a journey," he told it. "Hold on tight, even though you haven't got any hands."

They walked all day.

Tobi learned a new way of walking: one leg, then the other, without jolting anything, like carrying water in a leaf. When there was a root, he went over it ever so slowly. When there was mud, he went round it.

"Hurry up, Tobi!" Cresta shouted from the front. "You're slower than a sleepy snail!"

Tobi didn't answer. So as not to lose the rhythm, he counted his steps.

In the evening, the path began to climb. The ferns got smaller. The rocks, enormous.

And in front of them, between two towering walls of rock, opened a narrow, twisting passage of stone.

"That's the gorge," said Grandma Duna. "The plateaus are on the other side. We have to go through one at a time."

The gorge was as narrow as a corridor. High up above, there was a thin stripe of sky. Between the rocks whistled the wind.

Tobi went in last, holding the egg so tightly against his chest that he could feel his own heartbeat bouncing off the shell.

"One," he said to himself. "Two. Three."

One step for each number, without hurrying.

And then, halfway through, a stone came loose under his foot.

Tobi slipped. He fell on his side. And the egg flew out of his arms.

Tobi saw it all very slowly: the egg in the air, the egg hitting the ground, the egg rolling towards a deep, dark hole.

Tobi got up as best he could and ran, even though his knee was scraped, even though there was dust in his eyes.

He stretched his neck. He stretched it further. He stretched it as far as it would go.

And with the very tip of his snout, he stopped the egg right at the edge.

He stayed there, trembling, his heart pounding.

Then he hugged it with both front legs.

"Sorry," he said, his voice all wobbly. "Sorry, sorry. I'll never let go of you again."

And from inside, the egg answered with a gentle little tap. As if it were saying: it's all right.

On the other side of the gorge, the world opened up, wide and golden.

There were plateaus of soft grass and low trees full of new shoots. And at the top of a little hill, Tobi found the perfect spot: a hollow of warm earth, sheltered by three big rocks, looking out over the whole new valley.

He worked until night fell. He gathered dry leaves, moss and a few feathers he found lying around, and he made the softest nest he had ever made.

He put the egg in the middle and curled up around it, like a doughnut.

"We made it," he said. "We're home."

And for the first time in many days, he slept deeply, without waking once.

The next morning, Tobi was woken by a crack.

First a tiny one. Then a longer one. And the shell opened like a window.

Out came a head.

But it wasn't a long-necked head like Tobi's. It was tiny, with a curved beak, soft cinnamon-coloured feathers and two round eyes that looked straight at him.

"Peep," it said.

Tobi's chest filled up with something so big it hardly fitted inside.

Cresta and Roco came running.

"But it's a bird!" shouted Roco. "It's not like you, Tobi! It's not your family!"

Tobi lowered his snout, let the chick climb up onto his head, and answered very calmly:

"She's mine. I looked after her from the river. Her name is Pluma."

In the days that followed, Tobi had to learn all over again, from the very beginning.

He learned that Pluma didn't eat ferns, but seeds and little bugs, and he helped her look for them in the grass. He learned that she liked to sleep on top of his neck. He learned that when she was cold, she peeped very softly.

And he learned that he loved her just the same. Exactly the same, even though they looked nothing alike.

One evening, Grandma Duna sat down beside him.

"Do you know something, Tobi? Family isn't the ones who look like you. Family is the ones who stay."

That night, Pluma snuggled into the warm hollow of Tobi's neck.

Tobi breathed slowly, the way he had when he was looking after the egg. And like that, close and cosy, the two of them fell asleep.
